subject: missing data when axis limits set

messages.author: 9783d9fe56013431
messages.subject: missing data when axis limits set
parts:
Hi,
I have data that ranges from 0 to 0.02 on the y axis and I want to
zoom in on a few plots so that only the data from 0 to 0.01 is viewed.
I do this using ylim(0, 0.01) but when I use this, the geom_line
plotted values that fall above the ylimit disappear entirely rather
than just hitting the top of the plot. Is there a way to avoid losing
these extreme values?
Thank you,
squid.

messages.author: 66a7bbbceef834e9
messages.subject: Re: missing data when axis limits set
parts:
Hey,
you can do that with scale_y_continous(limits=c(0,0.01))
Here's an example from the book to make it clearer:

p <- qplot(disp, wt, data=mtcars) + geom_smooth()
p + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(325, 500))

Luciano

messages.author: 434226b3d3677f6e
messages.subject: Re: missing data when axis limits set
parts:
Hi,

This doesn't address the issue.. for me, this is my main complaint
about ggplot, and I'm not sure how to get around it. It's an issue
with geom_area and geom_line (and presumably _freqpoly), but not R's
native plotting engines.

Here is an example scenario:

t$x <- seq(100)
t$y <- dnorm(t$x, mean=50, sd=10)
ggplot(t) + geom_area(aes(x, y))

That looks like a perfectly normal bell curve. Now add either ylim
(0,0.02) or scale_y_continuous(limits=c(0,0.02)) into the mix and look
at what you get. Two spikes with emptiness in the middle.

It's really quite misleading on a number of levels. Depending on what
the data looks like, your eye may be lead to believe that it's
plotting zero values instead of "off the chart" values. Even it's
clear that it is not plotting zeroes, it is at the very least
suggesting that you have missing data in those regions... but my input
did not contain any NAs.. there really are plottable values there.

Omitting the out-of-range values (and complaining that you "missed
some data points due to small ylim range") is okay for geom_point, but
not for geom_area or geom_line (especially geom_area).

I suppose the data could be fed through some home-made range-limiting
function before passing it to ggplot, but even that would be somewhat
misleading for, say, situations where we had much less data points.
The slope of the line going off the page would potentially not be
steep enough in some situations.

I am using ggplot2_0.8.2 on R 2.8.1 GUI 1.27 Tiger build 32-bit
(5301). Perhaps this isn't an issue in other versions or platforms?

Thanks,

No, there aren't - because you've restricted the scale to exclude
them. You probably want the xlim and ylim arguments to
coord_cartesian to zoom into the region of interest.

Interesting... thank you everyone for all the feedback. Both
solutions worked: using coord_cartesian (instead of ylim/
scale_y_continuous) plots geom_area and geom_line the way I would
expect. And upgrading my R and ggplot to the latest versions make
ylim/scale_y_continuous produce the same output as Stefan... though
interestingly, the coord_cartesian plot is cleaner, because it
actually shows data going off the chart, whereas the ylim/
scale_y_continuous plots look truncated just short of the specified
range.

messages.author: 9e1d805a26f6d719
messages.subject: Re: missing data when axis limits set
parts:
Right, this is a slightly unintuitive aspect of ggplot. The scale_
(limits=) syntax restricts the *data* (as do its unfortunately named
synonyms xlim and ylim), while the coord_(xlim=) syntax restricts the
*viewport*. Scale_ functions affects the mapping between data and
plot, while coord_ functions just change the plot. In retrospect, some
of these functions and parameters perhaps should have been named
something else...

-Harlan

> But how could the scales work any other way?  If you set
> scale_colour_discrete(limits = c("a", "b")) you don't expect "c" and
> "d" to some how influence the display of the plot, do you?

You don't, and when I think about it, I don't, but people who aren't
experts with ggplot don't yet have a clear understanding of what
"scale" does. Also, it's the first graphing system I've ever used that
lets you restrict the data that way (versus a "subset" type of
command). So, if you're trying to map ggplot's syntax onto your
existing mental models of graphing programs, you're going to assume
that scale_x_continuous(limits=c(1,10)) is going to affect the axis,
not the data. It says "x", and doesn't say "data", so that's a pretty
natural assumption! And the xlim() function is even more likely to be
mapped that way in your head.

>
> > while the coord_(xlim=) syntax restricts the

I agree! Not sure what the solution is...

-Harlan

mainly a problem because the grammar incorporates statistical
transformations, and changes to the data implied by the scale must be
applied before the statistical transformation (which is why it isn't
so much a problem for geoms with the identity stat).
